title: Data Structures and Algorithms
description: Big-O, core data structures and classic algorithms for interviews and beyond

questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the search range each step, so it needs about log₂(n) comparisons.

questions.question: Which data structure follows Last In, First Out (LIFO) order?
questions.explanation: A stack removes the most recently added item first. A queue is First In, First Out.

questions.question: What is the average time complexity of a lookup in a hash table?
questions.explanation: With a good hash function and low load factor, lookups average O(1). Many collisions can degrade the worst case to O(n).

questions.question: What is quicksort's worst-case time complexity?
questions.explanation: Quicksort averages O(n log n) but degrades to O(n²) when pivots are consistently poor, for example the first element of an already sorted array.

questions.question: Which traversal visits a binary search tree's nodes in ascending order?
questions.explanation: In-order traversal visits left subtree, node, then right subtree, which yields a BST's keys in sorted order.

questions.question: Which algorithm finds shortest paths from one source in a graph with non-negative edge weights?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm greedily settles the closest unvisited node. Kruskal's finds a minimum spanning tree instead.

questions.question: Which data structure does breadth-first search use to track nodes to visit?
questions.explanation: BFS uses a FIFO queue so nodes are explored level by level. Depth-first search uses a stack, often via recursion.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of merge sort in every case?
questions.explanation: Merge sort always splits in half (log n levels) and merges each level in O(n), giving O(n log n) for best, average and worst cases.

questions.question: In a binary min-heap, where is the smallest element?
questions.explanation: The heap property keeps every parent no larger than its children, so the minimum is always at the root and can be read in O(1).

questions.question: What technique stores solutions to overlapping subproblems to avoid recomputing them?
questions.explanation: Dynamic programming caches subproblem results (memoization or tabulation). For example, it turns naive exponential Fibonacci into O(n).
